pos: n. (the town of Haruz, whose daughter was mother of king Amon)
etymology: Hebrew Yotbah, pleasantness, or goodness, from tob, good; named once, 2 Kings 21:19.
biblical_def: Jotbah is named once, as the home town of a king's grandfather: “Amon was twenty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Meshullemeth, the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah” (2 Kings 21:19). The verdict on the reign follows at once: “And he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD, as his father Manasseh did” (2 Kings 21:20). Amon is one of the shortest and worst reigns in Judah's history — two years, idolatry inherited whole from his father, and death by conspiracy in his own house. Jotbah's location is not identified; it is distinct from Jotbathah, the wilderness encampment of Numbers and Deuteronomy, which lay in the Arabah far to the south. The name means pleasantness. A woman from a town called Pleasant bore the king who sacrificed to the carved images his father had made and forsook the LORD God of his fathers. What makes the notice bearable is what came next: Amon's son was Josiah, who at eight years old began the most thorough reformation in the history of the kingdom. Jotbah is the grandmother's town of Judah's worst king and the great-grandmother's town of its best.

And the servants of Amon conspired against him, and slew the king in his own house.
Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty and one years in Jerusalem. And his mother's name was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath.
corruption_summary: Generational sin is treated as destiny; Amon copied his father exactly, and Amon's own son broke the pattern at eight years old.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic religion speaks of generational curses and family systems as though a man's spiritual condition were determined by his inheritance, and there is enough truth in the observation to make the error dangerous. Amon did as his father Manasseh did; Scripture says so plainly. But Manasseh himself repented at the end, humbling himself greatly before the God of his fathers in Babylon, and Amon's son Josiah turned to the LORD with all his heart while still a boy. Three generations, three different ends.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that each man answers for his own sin, as Ezekiel 18 labours to establish against the proverb about the fathers' sour grapes, and that regeneration is God's sovereign work and not a family trait. The LORD visits iniquity and He also breaks the chain where He pleases. A town named Pleasant gave Judah a queen mother, and what came of her house was decided one soul at a time.

pos: n. (the Ephraimite town of Jeroboam the son of Nebat)
etymology: Hebrew Tseredah, the cooling, or a piercing, from a root signifying to pierce or to be cool; named once, 1 Kings 11:26.
biblical_def: Zereda is named once, and its one claim on the record is the man who came from it: “And Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon's servant, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow woman, even he lifted up his hand against the king” (1 Kings 11:26). Everything in the verse matters. He was an Ephraimite, of the tribe that would lead the northern secession; he was Solomon's own servant, promoted for his industry to be ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph; his mother was a widow; and he lifted up his hand against the king. The LORD had already told him by Ahijah the Shilonite that ten tribes would be given him, and had attached a promise: if he would walk in God's ways and keep His statutes, God would build him a sure house as He built for David. Jeroboam received the kingdom and refused the condition. He made two calves of gold, set them in Bethel and Dan, said Behold thy gods, O Israel, and ordained a feast and a priesthood of his own devising. The phrase the sin of Jeroboam becomes the standing measure of apostasy for every northern king after him.

Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
And he shall give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, who did sin, and who made Israel to sin.
corruption_summary: Jeroboam's calves are excused as a cultural contextualising of Israel's worship; Scripture names them the sin that destroyed the northern kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeroboam did not announce a new god. He said, Behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt — claiming to represent the LORD who did the exodus, in a form the people would find accessible and in locations more convenient than Jerusalem. That is contextualisation, and Scripture calls it the sin whereby he made Israel to sin. The modern parallel needs no drawing out: worship redesigned for reach, with the God of the Bible still named over it.

The regulative principle is the safeguard, and the Second Commandment is its ground. God had appointed one place, one altar, one priesthood and one order of feasts, and Jeroboam altered every one of them for reasons of state. He had been given an explicit promise of a sure house on condition of obedience, and he traded it. A town called Zereda in the hills of Ephraim is remembered for producing the man by whom the measure of Israel's apostasy is named.

pos: n. (a son of Shimon in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Rinnah, a shout, a song, or joyful crying, from ranan, to shout for joy; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:20.
biblical_def: Rinnah is the second of the four sons of Shimon: “And the sons of Shimon were, Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth” (1 Chronicles 4:20). He has no recorded deed and no traced descendant. What he has is a name that is one of the great words of the Psalter. Rinnah is the Hebrew for a shout of joy, the word that stands in the promise of the sowers: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him” (Psalm 126:6). A man in the tribe of Judah was named Joyful-Shout, and the Chronicler put him in the register of households entitled to a portion in the land. The chapter he stands in is the densest stretch of Judahite genealogy in Scripture, and it is the tribe of the sceptre; the shout his name carries belongs, in the end, to the King who came out of it. Of Rinnah himself, Scripture preserves the name and the family and nothing else.

corruption_summary: Joy in worship is reduced to produced emotion; the biblical word is a shout grounded in what God has actually done.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern worship frequently treats joy as an atmosphere to be generated — a function of volume, lighting, and momentum. The Hebrew word that names this man appears in the Psalms attached to causes: the LORD hath done great things for us, the captivity turned, the sheaves brought home after the weeping. Biblical rejoicing is a response to accomplished fact, which is why it can coexist with grief and why it does not need to be manufactured.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's joy rests on finished work, not on present feeling. The sower weeps on the way out and shouts on the way back because the harvest is real. A man named Joyful-Shout in an unexplained verse of 1 Chronicles bears a word the whole Psalter uses for the noise God's people make when they consider what He has done.

pos: n. (the fourth son of Shimon in the genealogy of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Tilon, a mound, or possibly a gift, of uncertain derivation; named once, 1 Chronicles 4:20.
biblical_def: Tilon closes the list of Shimon's sons: “And the sons of Shimon were, Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi were, Zoheth, and Benzoheth” (1 Chronicles 4:20). Four brothers in half a verse, and then the register turns to another household in the same line. Nothing is recorded of Tilon beyond his father's name and his place in the order of birth, and the sense of his own name is not certain. He stands in the fourth chapter of 1 Chronicles, which traces the tribe of Judah through its lesser households after the royal line has been given in chapter three. The purpose is title: who belonged to Judah, and therefore who had a claim in Judah's portion when the exiles came back to a ruined country and had to sort out whose field was whose. A dictionary that aims to define every word in the Authorized Version must define this one too, and the definition is short because the record is. Tilon was a real man in the tribe out of which Christ came, and the word of God preserved his name when it preserved nothing else about him.

corruption_paragraphs: The objection to entries like this one is practical: what is the use of a name about which nothing is known? The answer is the use the Chronicler put it to. The genealogies of Judah are the documentation of a tribe, and the New Testament rests an argument on that documentation — it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda, says the writer to the Hebrews, in the course of proving that the priesthood had changed. The evidence for that evidence is lists like this.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's work in history is carried by people whose lives were not remarkable and whose names He nevertheless wrote down. The believer's comfort is not that his deeds will be recounted but that his name is known: “I know my sheep, and am known of mine” is the whole of it, and Tilon is in the book.

pos: n. (a Reubenite, father of Adina the captain)
etymology: Hebrew Shiza, of uncertain sense; taken by some as splendour, or as a shortened theophoric; named once, 1 Chronicles 11:42.
biblical_def: Shiza is named once, as the father of a captain: “Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain of the Reubenites, and thirty with him” (1 Chronicles 11:42). The verse falls in the long tail of the roll of David's mighty men, in the section the Chronicler adds beyond the list preserved in 2 Samuel — the men from the eastern tribes and from beyond Jordan. Adina brought thirty of his own with him, which marks him a chief of a company rather than a lone champion, and his father's name and tribe are given so the house could be identified. Reuben was Jacob's firstborn and lost the birthright for the sin recorded in Genesis 35; the tribe settled east of Jordan, was reproached in Deborah's song for staying by its sheepfolds while others fought, and is not heard from much afterwards. Yet when David came to the throne, a Reubenite captain and thirty men stood in the muster. Shiza is remembered for having raised him. It is the ordinary way the word of God preserves a man: not for what he did, but as the father of someone who turned up when the anointed king needed men.

corruption_paragraphs: Reuben's record is poor. The firstborn forfeited the birthright, the tribe chose its inheritance on the wrong side of the river, and Deborah's song asks why Reuben abode among the sheepfolds when the LORD's people went to war. It would be easy to close the account there, as commentators sometimes do. First Chronicles 11 does not: it names Adina the son of Shiza the Reubenite, a captain with thirty men, standing with David.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's dealings with a family or a tribe are not exhausted by its worst chapter. The LORD had said of Reuben that he should not die, even in the sentence that stripped his excellency, and Revelation 7 numbers Reuben among the sealed. A father from the tribe that stayed home raised a son who came.

pos: n. (a prince of Babylon present at the fall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Of Babylonian form, taken as be gracious, O Nebo, or sword of Nebo, from the name of the Babylonian god Nebo; named once, Jeremiah 39:3.
biblical_def: Samgar-nebo is one of the Babylonian officers who took possession of Jerusalem: “And all the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate, even Nergalsharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim, Rabsaris, Nergalsharezer, Rabmag, with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon” (Jeremiah 39:3). The date is given in the verse above: “And in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, the city was broken up” (Jeremiah 39:2). The detail is that of an eyewitness: the exact year, month and day, the named officers, and the particular spot where they sat down — the middle gate, the place where a city's business and judgment were transacted. Babylon's princes sat in the gate of Jerusalem, holding court in the city of the great King. The name Samgar-nebo invokes Nebo, the Babylonian god of writing and wisdom, the deity Isaiah had mocked in advance: Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth. A man named for Nebo sat in Jerusalem's gate the day the city fell, and within seventy years Babylon itself was a ruin and the LORD had sent His people home.

corruption_summary: The fall of Jerusalem is read as the failure of Israel's God; the prophets had announced it in advance as His act, and named the deliverance that would follow.
corruption_paragraphs: The destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon is the ancient world's standing argument that the God of Israel was weaker than the gods of the empire, and critical scholarship reproduces a version of it by treating Israel's theology as improvised after the disaster. Jeremiah had been preaching the disaster for forty years before it happened, had been imprisoned for saying the city would be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and had bought a field in Anathoth as a signed testimony that houses and fields would be possessed again in that land.

Scripture presents Nebuchadnezzar as the LORD's servant in this and Babylon as a rod that would itself be broken. Isaiah had named Nebo stooping and Bel bowing down, and Cyrus by name a century and a half before he issued the decree. The principle to recover is that God governs the empires that chasten His people and sets the term of their power. The princes who sat in the middle gate were executing a sentence passed in heaven, and their own city's sentence was already written.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Zephon, a clan of the tribe of Gad)
etymology: Hebrew Tsephoni, of Zephon, the watchman or the northern, from tsaphah, to look out or keep watch; named once, Numbers 26:15.
biblical_def: The Zephonites head the list of Gadite families in the census of the plains of Moab: “The children of Gad after their families: of Zephon, the family of the Zephonites: of Haggi, the family of the Haggites: of Shuni, the family of the Shunites” (Numbers 26:15). Seven families of Gad are named in that chapter, and the tribe's total comes to forty thousand and five hundred. The name is built on the Hebrew for keeping watch, and Gad was a tribe that had to keep it: their portion lay east of Jordan, on the exposed frontier toward Ammon and the desert, which is why Moses bound them by oath to cross over armed before their brethren and fight until the western tribes had rest. Jacob had said of Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last, and Moses blessed him as one that dwelleth as a lion. The Zephonites are named once and never described. They were among the households that took the exposed ground, sent their fighting men across the river first, and came back to a border that would be raided for the next six hundred years.

But the account does not end in rebuke. They bound themselves by oath: We will pass over armed before the LORD to war, and the inheritance of our possession on this side Jordan may be ours. And they kept it, and Joshua dismissed them with a blessing years later.

pos: n. (the name of two men in the genealogy of Christ in Luke)
etymology: Greek Mattathias, for the Hebrew Mattithyah, gift of the LORD, from mattanah, a gift, with Yah; named twice, Luke 3:25 and Luke 3:26.
biblical_def: Mattathias is borne by two distinct men within two verses of the same genealogy: “Which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Amos, which was the son of Naum, which was the son of Esli, which was the son of Nagge” (Luke 3:25), and then one generation further back, “Which was the son of Maath, which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Semei, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Juda” (Luke 3:26). The name means gift of the LORD, the Greek form of the Hebrew Mattithiah. Both men stand in the stretch of Luke's descent running from Zerubbabel down toward Joseph — the four centuries between the Testaments, where no narrative survives and only the names are kept. Luke traces his line through Nathan the son of David rather than through Solomon, which is why his list diverges from Matthew's and why it reaches back past Abraham to Adam, which was the son of God. These are the generations nobody can tell a story about. Two men in them were named Gift-of-the-LORD, and the Gift they were in line for was still four hundred years off.

corruption_summary: The two genealogies of Christ are called a contradiction; Matthew traces the legal line through Solomon and Luke the natural descent through Nathan.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew and Luke give different lines between David and Joseph, and this is the most frequently cited discrepancy in the New Testament. The historic answer is straightforward and has been held since the fathers: Matthew gives the royal and legal succession through Solomon, establishing Christ's title to the throne, while Luke gives the natural descent through Nathan another son of David. Luke also begins with the careful phrase that Jesus was as was supposed the son of Joseph, flagging the virgin birth at the head of his list.

The two lines serve two arguments. Matthew writes to show the King of Israel in the line of the kings; Luke writes to show the Son of Man descended to Adam, which was the son of God, and therefore a Saviour for the nations. Neither evangelist is careless, and neither is inventing: both are working documents a first-century Jewish reader could check. Two obscure men named Gift-of-the-LORD in Luke's silent centuries are part of what made the claim checkable.

pos: n. (a family of the Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Tamach, laughter, or possibly combat; spelled Tamah at Nehemiah 7:55; named once in this form, Ezra 2:53.
biblical_def: Thamah heads a household among the temple servants who came back from the captivity: “The children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, the children of Thamah” (Ezra 2:53). Nehemiah's parallel register spells it Tamah: “The children of Barkos, the children of Sisera, the children of Tamah” (Nehemiah 7:55). These are the Nethinim — the given ones, the lowest order of temple servants, descended in part from the Gibeonites whom Joshua made hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. Their families are listed by name, household by household, alongside the priests and Levites and the men of the towns of Judah. That is the striking thing about Ezra 2. A people returning to rebuild a ruined temple counted its woodcutters and water-carriers as carefully as its priests, and the Holy Ghost preserved both lists. One of the households named in the same verse is the children of Sisera — a name that had belonged to the Canaanite captain Barak destroyed. Thamah's descendants came up out of Babylon to serve in the house of the LORD, and their father's name is in the Bible for it.

corruption_summary: Menial service in the house of God is counted beneath notice; Ezra's register names the woodcutters' households beside the priests'.
corruption_paragraphs: Every church has an unspoken hierarchy of visible ministry, and the Nethinim are the biblical rebuke to it. They were the lowest rank of the temple establishment, descended from a people who had entered the covenant by a ruse and been assigned the heavy work for it, and Ezra counts their families by name on the return from exile. Scripture spends verses on the genealogy of men whose job was to carry wood and draw water.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God records the service nobody watches. The Psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness, and the doorkeepers are in the register. A household named Thamah came four months across the desert from Babylon to do the lowest work in a temple that was not yet built.

pos: n. (a son of Jeconiah, of the royal house of Judah in captivity)
etymology: Hebrew Yeqamyah, the LORD will raise up, or Jehovah establishes, from qum, to arise or to stand, with Yah; named once, 1 Chronicles 3:18.
biblical_def: Jecamiah is the fourth of the six sons of Jeconiah: “Malchiram also, and Pedaiah, and Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah” (1 Chronicles 3:18). With this name the list of that household is complete in the dictionary: Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah, the sons of the king Babylon carried away at eighteen. Jeconiah is Jehoiachin, who reigned three months, did evil in the sight of the LORD, and spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison before Evil-merodach lifted up his head and set his throne above the throne of the kings that were with him in Babylon. These six sons were born to a captive king. Jecamiah's name is a statement of hope against the whole situation: the LORD will raise up. There was nothing in the circumstances to support it. The dynasty was broken, the city burned, the temple in ruins, the royal family eating at a foreign table by permission. And the LORD did raise up — through this family's line, by way of Salathiel and Zerubbabel, down to a village carpenter and the Child he named Jesus.

corruption_summary: The exile is read as the end of the Davidic hope; the books of Kings close on a captive king lifted out of prison and seated at a table.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Kings ends in what looks like failure: the temple burned, the people deported, the land emptied. Its final paragraph is therefore one of the most deliberate endings in Scripture. In the seven and thirtieth year of the captivity, Evil-merodach king of Babylon lifted up the head of Jehoiachin out of prison, changed his prison garments, and he did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life. The historian closes the book on a son of David alive, out of chains, eating at a king's table.

That is not sentiment; it is the thread the Davidic promise hangs by at its thinnest. Jecamiah was one of the sons in that household, and his name says what the chapter demonstrates: the LORD will raise up. The principle to recover is that God's promises survive the destruction of everything that seemed to carry them. A throne, a city and a temple were all lost, and the covenant was not.
